title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Chippewa County leaders consider a one-year moratorium on new data centers today.

lines.text: Good evening and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
Tonight we're starting with breaking news out of the eastern Upper Peninsula.
Chippewa County is the latest rural area to hit pause on new data centers.
Exactly. County leaders are weighing a temporary moratorium that would stop fresh proposals while they study impacts on land, power, and local services.
This comes as interest grows across Michigan's rural counties. Why Chippewa now, and what does it tell us about the bigger picture?
It's part of a clear pattern we've seen this week. Delta County already voted a one-year ban on Thursday after residents raised noise, water, and grid concerns.
Garfield Township did the same on Friday after a sloppy project filing. Calhoun County is debating a year-long halt over jobs versus power strain.
Right. These aren't isolated votes. They're responses to hyperscale projects that can pull hundreds of megawatts and millions of gallons of water daily.
So what's the history here? Why are so many townships and counties moving at once?
Rural Michigan has cheap land and available power in some spots, which attracts tech firms building for AI demand. But locals are realizing the trade-offs hit fast.
Power is the big one. How does one of these facilities affect electric bills?
A single large campus can equal the load of a small city. Utilities then need new lines or upgrades, and those costs often get spread across all ratepayers unless special deals are struck.
We've seen that tension in other stories this week. Indiana Michigan Power pledged on Saturday not to pass data center costs to residential customers in southwest Michigan.
Yes, and DTE's Q2 preview on Friday highlighted data center growth as a profit driver, which raises questions about who pays for the added infrastructure.
What about water? These places use massive amounts for cooling.
Cooling towers can draw millions of gallons a day. In rural areas that rely on wells or limited municipal systems, that creates real competition with farms and homes.
And farmland itself. These projects often go on open land that could stay agricultural.
Exactly. Once built, the tax base shifts, but so does the character of the township. Residents worry about noise from cooling systems too.
We heard about that in Dowagiac on Thursday. People are already dealing with humming from an operating facility and exploring legal options.
That ongoing noise complaint shows the issues don't end at construction. They continue for years.
So what happens next in Chippewa? They study impacts and then what?
They'll likely draft permanent zoning rules, decide on setbacks, noise limits, and tax agreements. Other counties that paused are doing the same right now.
Could development just shift to places without moratoriums?
That's the risk. Some projects might look at Washtenaw County or other areas still open, like the Oracle proposal in Augusta Township that's up for a vote soon.
Augusta is deciding on zoning and tax terms for a large DTE-connected project. The outcome there will show how much revenue townships can actually capture.
Meanwhile Saline Township reversed an earlier limit on incentives for Oracle after company lobbying. That flip shows how these decisions can swing quickly.
And the Senate candidates weighed in yesterday on protecting ratepayers from transmission costs. Different plans on whether utilities or tech firms should cover upgrades.
Primary voters now see concrete differences on an issue that directly hits monthly bills.
Stepping back, how many places have paused so far?
At least five counties or townships in the last week alone. It's a fast-moving local response to rapid interest.
What should listeners watch for in Chippewa over the next month?
Public hearings on the moratorium language, resident input sessions, and any new applications that test the pause.
And across the state, how utilities respond in rate cases will matter a lot.
Agreed. Now let's move to the other stories from this week in quick hits.
Starting with the Senate primary. Democratic candidates split on data center power costs yesterday.
They laid out different approaches to regulating demand and shielding ratepayers from new transmission expenses.
That gives voters clear contrasts on who pays when AI demand spikes.
Next, Indiana Michigan Power's pledge on Saturday.
The utility serving southwest Michigan promised residential customers won't foot the bill for new data center lines.
Consumer groups are watching to see if that holds in future rate cases.
DTE's earnings preview on Friday highlighted data centers as a profit driver.
More demand means more infrastructure pressure, and Michigan ratepayers have already seen added charges from similar projects.
Calhoun County is also debating a year-long moratorium over electricity strain and whether jobs will benefit local taxpayers.
A pause there would delay projects drawing hundreds of megawatts and millions of gallons of water.
Augusta Township is nearing a vote on rules for an Oracle-scale project pulling from the same DTE territory as Saline.
The decision will shape how much new load hits ratepayers and what revenue the township keeps.
Dowagiac residents reported ongoing noise from an operating data center on Thursday.
Cooling systems are causing sleep issues, and some are exploring legal steps.
Saline Township flipped its position on tax breaks for the Oracle campus after lobbying.
Residents now face the prospect of forgoing years of property tax revenue on a multibillion-dollar project.
And Delta County already enacted its one-year ban on Thursday.
That gives officials time to write permanent zoning before any large projects move forward.
Lots of local action this week.
Now for on deck.
We're not tracking any major public meetings scheduled for tomorrow yet.
Listeners can check the Michigan Data Center Tracker for updates as agendas post.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker.
We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Chippewa County Weighs Data Center Freeze as Rural Michigan Pushes Back on Power and Water
